newsitem.title: UK: OECD sees stable UK inflation,small 97 rate rise.
newsitem.headline: OECD sees stable UK inflation,small 97 rate rise.

text.p: Britain's chances of achieving sustained growth and low inflation are the best for 30 years but interest rates will have to rise next year to keep price pressures at bay, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) said in its latest Economic Outlook.

"Cost pressures are expected to remain under control as average earnings growth remains modest, productivity growth remains healthy and monetary policy is firm," it said in its twice-yearly report, released on Monday.
The Paris-based think-tank said inflation could stabilise in the two to 2.5 percent range in 1997/98. Underlying annual inflation was 3.3 percent in November, above the 2.5 percent government target.

The OECD's year-end economic outlook, reviewing growth in its 27 member countires, was due to be published on December 19 but the organisation allowed the early release of the report after an international magazine broke the embargo.
"The OECD Secretariat projections assume a further small rise in base rates in the second half of 1997 to lock in low inflation levels," the report said.
"Such action would be a prudent response to above trend economic growth projected in the coming two years."
The OECD forecast gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 3.3 percent in 1997 and 3.0 percent in 1998 but said sterling's appreciation could have a dampening effect.
"Looking further ahead, private spending should be sustained by buoyant disposable incomess, recent tax cuts, low interest rates and other "windfall receipts'," the OECD said.
It said the risks surrounding its projections appeared balanced.

"On the upside, strong growth in the monetary aggregates could feed into stronger consumer spending and private investment. On the downside, a weaker than predicted recovery in continental Europe could spill over into lower exports and business confidence."
Unemployment, which was 7.2 percent of the workforce in October, could drop to below seven percent in 1998, the lowest level in eight years.
The OECD said fiscal consolidation had been proceeding less rapidly than planned because of sluggish growth and weaker than expected tax revenues.
"But significant further progress in delivering the planned reduction in public sector borrowing will be needed to achieve the government's medium-term balanced budget objective."

It projected general government net borrowing at around 3.7 percent of GDP in 1997, then falling in 1998 to 3.0 percent -- the level European Union countries must achieve to qualify to join a single European currency.
Gross debt is expected to stabilise in 1997/98 at slightly above the 60 percent level stipulated in the Maastricht Treaty on European union.
